title: Certified Payroll in Texas: What Contractors Need to Know
summary: Texas certified payroll requirements for contractors. Covers Chapter 2258, prevailing wage rates, recordkeeping, penalties, and federal Davis-Bacon overlap.
body_markdown:
Texas doesn't get as much attention as states like California or New York when it comes to[prevailing wage compliance](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/state-prevailing-wage-laws-contractors) . But the state has its own prevailing wage law, and it applies to every public works project regardless of contract size. If you're a trade contractor working on state or locally funded construction in Texas,[certified payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/what-is-certified-payroll-contractor-guide) is part of the deal.


What makes Texas different is how the system works. There's no centralized filing portal, no single state form, and no statewide wage schedule. The contracting public body sets the rates, specifies the documentation, and enforces compliance. That decentralized structure creates real challenges for contractors working across multiple jurisdictions.


## **What Triggers Certified Payroll in Texas**


Here is a detailed explanation.


### **Texas Government Code Chapter 2258**


Texas prevailing wage requirements are governed by Government Code Chapter 2258. The law requires that workers on public works projects funded by the state or local government be paid at least the prevailing wage rate for their trade classification in the locality where the work is performed.


There is no minimum dollar threshold. Unlike the federal Davis-Bacon Act, which kicks in at $2,000, Chapter 2258 applies to all covered public works contracts regardless of value. Every contractor and subcontractor on the project must comply.


### **Federal Davis-Bacon Overlap**


When a Texas project receives federal funding, the Davis-Bacon Act may apply in addition to Chapter 2258. Federal projects over $2,000 must meet federal[prevailing wage](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/what-is-prevailing-wage-davis-bacon-guide) standards and file certified payroll using Form WH-347.


When both apply, follow the higher wage standard. Recordkeeping obligations are similar, but wage determinations, classification systems, and[fringe benefit calculations](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/how-to-calculate-prevailing-wage-fringe-benefits) may differ.


## **How Prevailing Wage Rates Are Set in Texas**


This is where Texas diverges from most other states. There is no statewide wage schedule published by a central labor department. Instead, the public body awarding the contract determines the prevailing rate for each trade classification on the project.


### **How Public Bodies Determine Rates**


The awarding agency researches actual wages paid on comparable construction in the locality. Inputs include local collective bargaining agreements, regional wage surveys, contractor input, and DOL-published rates for the area.


### **What This Means for Contractors**


Rates can vary from one city to the next, and from one agency to the next within the same city. A school district project in Houston may use different rates than a TxDOT highway project in the same county. Confirm the specific wage determination for each project before bidding.


Wage determinations must be posted visibly at the jobsite.


## **Certified Payroll and Recordkeeping Requirements**


### **No Standard State Form**


Texas does not mandate a specific certified payroll form. The contracting public body specifies documentation requirements in the project specifications. In practice, most agencies accept the federal WH-347 form, and many require it by default.


Regardless of form, contractors must maintain records that include:


-


Worker names and trade classifications


-


Hours worked per day and per week


-


Wages paid (including overtime)


-


Fringe benefits provided


### **Filing and Retention**


The submission schedule depends on the awarding agency. Some require weekly filing. Others require payroll on request or at set intervals.


Prime contractors are responsible for ensuring subs maintain their own records and comply with the wage determination. Joint liability applies. If a sub underpays, the prime is accountable.


Records must be available for inspection during the project and retained afterward per the contract. Even when retention isn't specified, keeping[payroll records](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll-reports) for at least three years is standard practice.


### **Overtime Rules**


Texas follows the standard overtime rule: time-and-a-half for hours over 40 in a workweek. On Chapter 2258 projects, overtime may also apply for hours over 8 in a single day. The overtime rate is calculated on the base prevailing wage, with fringe benefit cash payments excluded from the regular rate.


## **Penalties for Non-Compliance**


Texas treats prevailing wage violations as a per-worker, per-day penalty:


-


**$60 per worker for each calendar day** (or part of a day) that a worker is paid below the prevailing rate


-


Back wages owed to underpaid workers


-


Potential debarment from future public contracts


-


Contract termination for material breach


-


Joint liability between prime contractors and subcontractors


Workers who report violations are protected from retaliation. Employers cannot pay below the prevailing rate even with worker consent.


The $60 daily penalty may sound modest, but it compounds. Ten workers underpaid for 20 working days is $12,000 in penalties alone, before back wages.


## **Where Texas Contractors Get Tripped Up**


### **Assuming No State Prevailing Wage Applies**


Texas is sometimes grouped with states that have no prevailing wage law. That's wrong. Chapter 2258 is active, and the absence of a centralized filing system doesn't mean the absence of requirements. Contractors who assume only Davis-Bacon matters miss the state layer.


### **Using the Wrong Wage Determination**


Because rates are set by the awarding body, contractors working across multiple Texas jurisdictions can't reuse rates from project to project. Each determination must be confirmed before payroll runs. A[payroll audit](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/how-to-run-a-construction-payroll-audit) run against the wrong determination produces compliant-looking records that aren't actually compliant.


### **Ignoring Subcontractor Compliance**


Joint liability means a sub's underpayment becomes the prime's problem. Contractors who don't[verify sub compliance](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/pre-bid-compliance-checklist-public-works-contractors) before the agency does are carrying risk they can't see.

## **FAQs**


### Does Texas have a prevailing wage law?


Yes. Texas Government Code Chapter 2258 requires prevailing wages on all state and locally funded public works projects, with no minimum contract threshold. Rates are set by the awarding public body, not a statewide schedule.


### What form do Texas contractors use for certified payroll?


Texas does not mandate a specific state form. The awarding agency specifies documentation requirements in the contract. Most agencies accept or require the federal WH-347 form.


### What are the penalties for prevailing wage violations in Texas?


$60 per worker for each calendar day of underpayment, plus back wages, potential debarment, and contract termination. Prime contractors and subcontractors share joint liability.


### How are prevailing wage rates determined in Texas?


The public body awarding the contract determines rates based on local wage surveys, collective bargaining agreements, and comparable project data. Rates can vary between agencies and jurisdictions, even within the same city.


### Do federal Davis-Bacon rules apply to Texas projects?


Davis-Bacon applies when a Texas project receives federal funding and exceeds $2,000 in contract value. When both state and federal requirements apply, contractors should follow the higher wage standard.


*This guide is for informational purposes only. Prevailing wage rates and certified payroll requirements in Texas vary by awarding agency and project. Consult the contracting public body or your compliance team for requirements specific to your project.*
